summary:
Section 210 of the Penal Code prohibits male same-sex sexual activity. Anal or oral sex, whether heterosexual or homosexual, is punishable as sodomy with up to 14 years' imprisonment, and other same-sex sexual acts carry up to three years. Sex between women is not restricted by law. As of 2024 there is no legal recognition of transgender or gender-diverse identities, and the criminal penalties attach to sexual acts rather than to transgender identity as such.

Enforcement is sporadic. No prosecutions directed at LGBTQ people were recorded in 2012, but arrests occurred in 2015 and 2022. In the 2015 case a man charged with indecent acts between males pleaded guilty and received a suspended sentence with community service and mandatory counselling; in 2022 two men were arrested after having sex. Decriminalisation was described as not a priority in 2011, and in 2023 the government confirmed it had no intention of repealing the laws criminalising male homosexuality, stating that existing protections against violence and abuse were sufficient.

The Asian Development Bank's 2024 assessment of the legal status of sexual and gender minorities in 17 countries in Asia and the Pacific includes Papua New Guinea, with decriminalisation among the topics examined. The criminal-law position is therefore a live question in regional legal review rather than a settled matter.

Violence against trans and gender-diverse people in Port Moresby is documented. Gay and transgender people in the capital are commonly raped or beaten, in some cases by police officers, according to reporting by the documentary maker Vlad Sokhin broadcast by ABC News in October 2014. A 2011 study found police were one of the main sources of violence against men who have sex with men and trans people. Abuse commonly continues even when reported, because of the imbalance of power between victims and police, and victims are often framed as perpetrators. A 24-year-old gay man described being pelted with stones and bottles.

Hanuabada, a village built over the sea on the outskirts of Port Moresby, functions as a sanctuary. Residents live openly there, and transgender people wear women's clothes in the street without retaliation. LGBTQ people subjected to violence elsewhere in the country, including in the capital, frequently move to the village.

Transgender Papua New Guineans use the Tok Pisin word palopa, reportedly derived from the name of the American singer Jennifer Lopez, for a cultural and traditional third gender, and the Sambia recognise a traditional third gender, kwolu-aatmwol, literally a male thing transforming into a female thing. The words lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender carry heavy stigma. LGBTQ people report discrimination in daily life and difficulty finding work. Homophobia is widespread, and homosexuality is more accepted in coastal areas than in the Highlands, although no source documents societal tolerance of transgender people specifically.
tangentialFactors:
Police accountability is weak across the board, which bears on what a trans visitor can expect if an assault is reported. Human Rights Watch reported in January 2009 that a mob stripped a woman accused of sorcery, beat her with hot iron rods and burned her within yards of a police station; provincial commanders recorded more than 50 sorcery-related killings in two highland provinces in 2008, with perpetrators rarely brought to justice. Sorcery accusations, often linked to HIV deaths, were used to conceal murders and to mitigate sentences, and police routinely took no action.

The Guardian reported in January 2017 on Human Rights Watch's annual assessment that police abuse in Papua New Guinea, including of children, continued to be reported with little accountability even for fatalities or egregious physical abuse. These findings concern the general enforcement climate rather than trans-specific targeting, but they indicate the low likelihood of a complaint being pursued.

LGBTQ people report discrimination in daily life and difficulty finding work, and the vocabulary for sexual and gender minorities carries heavy stigma.

Violence drives internal movement. Residents subjected to rape and assault in Port Moresby and elsewhere relocate to Hanuabada, which functions as a gay village and sanctuary where people live openly. outOfScopeNotes:
The sources state no transgender-specific rule on identity documents or markers, airport or police screening, detention and custody, facilities, or access to transition-related care. How the criminal provisions would be applied to a trans visitor, as distinct from the general prohibition on male same-sex acts, is not documented.

Prosecution data are limited to individual cases in 2012, 2015 and 2022; no systematic enforcement statistics were identified. The observation that homosexuality is more accepted in coastal areas than in the Highlands concerns LGBTQ people generally and is not documented as trans-specific.
